interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: Toward Auditable AI Scientists: A Hypothesis Evolution Protocol for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to play a central role in AI-driven scientific discovery. Equipped with broad knowledge, flexible reasoning, and tool use, they have the potential to autonomously explore and solve scientific problems by repeatedly proposing hypotheses, testing them, and revising their beliefs in the light of the evidence. In current agents, however, these hypotheses, tests, and belief updates are buried in unstructured logs, and no mechanism lets the agent or the human researcher audit that process. Here we propose the Hypothesis Evolution Protocol (HEP), an agent harness that provides hypothesis generation, evaluation, and evolution as explicit, auditable operations. On materials-science research tasks, a HEP-equipped agent operates the hypothesis--test--evidence--belief cycle that planning-style agents lack, generalizes across research questions, and exploits the protocol more fully as the base LLM becomes more capable. These results mark a step toward auditable AI scientists, whose scientific reasoning can be inspected, verified, and built upon.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses LLM agents for scientific discovery with a focus on auditability, which is highly relevant to automated research workflows in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper addresses the problem that LLM agents for scientific discovery lack auditability: their hypothesis generation, testing, and belief updates are buried in unstructured logs. The authors propose the Hypothesis Evolution Protocol (HEP), a framework that makes hypothesis generation, evaluation, and evolution explicit, auditable operations. This is highly relevant to astronomy because it provides a mechanism to inspect and verify an AI agent's reasoning when analyzing JWST data or building models of high-redshift galaxies. A concrete workflow could be using a HEP-equipped agent to propose and test hypotheses about the nature of little red dots (e.g., AGN vs. stellar populations) by querying SED-fitting codes and checking consistency with spectra. A key caveat is that the paper evaluates HEP on materials-science tasks, not astronomy, so the transferability to astronomical workflows needs to be validated.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the HEP protocol is general enough to be applied to hypothesis-driven tasks in astrophysics, such as SED fitting or spectral line identification.
Look for details on how the protocol handles uncertainty and conflicting evidence, which is common in astronomical data.
Examine the computational overhead and whether the protocol can be integrated with existing astronomical tools like CIGALE or Bagpipes.

papers.title: Task-Specific Multimodal Question Answering Agents via Confidence Calibration and Incremental Reasoning for QANTA 2026
papers.abstract: We present our submission to the QANTA 2026 shared challenge at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Efficient Multimodal Question Answering (EMM-QA). Quanta evaluates multimodal quizbowl systems that answer pyramid-style questions from incrementally revealed text and accompanying images while operating under realistic efficiency constraints. The challenge consists of two distinct tasks: Tossup questions, which require deciding when to answer under uncertainty, and Bonus questions, which emphasize accurate answer selection and human adoption. To address these differing objectives, we develop a task-specific two-agent architecture. Our Tossup agent utilizes a GPT-4o-mini-class model (referred to as GPT-4.1-mini in the competition logs) with confidence-calibrated answering and a domain-specific numeric reasoning policy that reduces overconfident predictions from isolated quantitative clues. Our Bonus agent uses GPT-4o-class model (referred to as GPT-4.1) with leadin-aware reasoning, structured relational reasoning, and multimodal evidence integration to improve exact answer selection. Rather than relying on a retrieval pipeline or model ensembles, our approach emphasizes efficient reasoning policies and confidence calibration within a hosted-only environment. Our system achieved the highest overall leaderboard score of 0.402, including a Tossup score of 0.238 and a Bonus Effect score of 0.164. The results demonstrate that lightweight, task-specific reasoning strategies can provide strong performance on resource-constrained multimodal question answering benchmarks.
papers.Reasons for match: This paper directly addresses multimodal question answering with confidence calibration and incremental reasoning, which are highly relevant for building research agents that answer astronomy questions by combining text, images, and data. The task-specific agent architecture and confidence calibration methods are transferable to scientific workflows.
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles the problem of answering multimodal quizbowl-style questions where information is revealed incrementally, requiring decisions about when to answer under uncertainty. The authors develop two agents: one for 'tossup' questions that uses confidence calibration to decide when to answer, and another for 'bonus' questions that uses structured reasoning and multimodal evidence integration. For astronomy, this is directly relevant because an astronomer could build a research agent that answers questions by combining text from papers, images from JWST, and tabular data from catalogs, while deciding when it has enough information to give a reliable answer. An astronomer could imagine using such an agent to answer questions like 'What is the redshift of this galaxy?' by querying multiple data sources and deciding when to stop gathering evidence. A key caveat is that the system is evaluated on a general knowledge quizbowl dataset, not on astronomy-specific questions, so its performance on scientific queries is unknown.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the confidence calibration method is described in enough detail to be implemented for a different domain, such as astronomy.
Look for the specific reasoning policies used for numeric and relational reasoning, as these could be adapted for astronomical measurements and relationships.
See if the paper discusses the computational cost of the agents, as this would affect feasibility for large-scale astronomy workflows.

papers.title: Promptable Concept Segmentation from Above: Evaluating SAM 3's Zero-Shot and One-Shot Capabilities in Remote Sensing
papers.abstract: The deployment of large-scale foundation models, such as the Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3), promises a transition toward open-vocabulary, training-free computer vision. However, their capacity to generalize out-of-distribution to the complex, top-down geometric structures of Earth Observation imagery remains largely unquantified. Driven by SAM 3's performance disparities in highly specialized domains, we present a comprehensive, multi-task empirical evaluation across remote sensing scene classification, object detection, and instance segmentation under strict zero-shot and one-shot constraints. To achieve this, we introduce a structural adaptation of SAM 3 by repurposing its decoupled binary presence head into a standalone zero-shot classifier. Furthermore, by systematically isolating textual and visual prompt modalities across five configurations, we explicitly diagnose the alignment mechanics within the model's multimodal decoder. Our findings reveal severe cross-modal interference: while visual prompts successfully align the decoder to complex remote sensing geometry, textual prompts inject misaligned, ground-level semantic bias, actively degrading coordinate regression. To benchmark these capabilities without resource-intensive training, we formulate a novel training-free proxy evaluation protocol for Generalized Zero-Shot tasks (scene classification and instance segmentation). Ultimately, our results demonstrate that SAM 3 avoids the overfitting commonly seen in legacy domain-adapted models, achieving high Harmonic Mean scores in segmentation tasks. However, it remains fundamentally constrained by sub-pixel resolution limits and overhead semantic blind spots, charting a definitive mandate for parameter-efficient geospatial fine-tuning of its multimodal decoder.
papers.Reasons for match: The paper evaluates SAM 3, a foundation model for segmentation, in remote sensing, which is directly analogous to astronomical image segmentation and source detection. The zero-shot and one-shot capabilities and the analysis of multimodal decoder alignment are relevant for adapting foundation models to JWST/astronomical imagery.
papers.Short digest: This paper asks whether the Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3), a large foundation model for image segmentation, can generalize to remote sensing imagery without additional training. The authors test SAM 3 on scene classification, object detection, and instance segmentation in zero-shot and one-shot settings, and find that visual prompts work well but textual prompts introduce bias. For astronomy, this matters because SAM-like models could be adapted to segment galaxies, detect sources, or deblend objects in JWST images without needing large labeled datasets. An astronomer could imagine testing SAM 3 on a few JWST images to see if it can identify galaxies or separate overlapping sources. A key caveat is that SAM 3 was trained on natural images, so its performance on astronomical data (with different noise, resolution, and object shapes) may be limited and may require fine-tuning.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the paper reports segmentation performance on overhead/remote sensing images with metrics like IoU or mAP, which would indicate how well the method might transfer to astronomical images.
Look for analysis of failure cases, especially those related to sub-pixel resolution or small objects, which are common in JWST data.
See if the paper discusses the computational cost or memory requirements for running SAM 3 on large images, relevant for survey-scale data.

papers.title: Multi-Conditioned Diffusion Synthesis of Sand Boils for Low-Resource Earthen-Levee Inspection
papers.authors: Padam Jung Thapa , Abdullah Bin Naeem , Ayon Dey , Anav Katwal , Md Tamjidul Hoque
papers.abstract: Sand boils on earthen levees are safety-critical defects, but pixel-level detection is limited by scarce annotations. We present a diffusion-based synthesis pipeline for low-resource sand-boil imagery. Using Stable Diffusion XL fine-tuned with DreamBooth and conditioned by a multi-branch ControlNet stack, the pipeline generates synthetic inspection images from a small curated reference set. A soft-mask inpainting protocol preserves the real defect pixels while re-rendering the surrounding scene, avoiding seams and color shifts from prior seamless-cloning compositing. A mask-conditioned ControlNet can also generate a new boil inside a chosen mask, making the mask the segmentation label by construction; however, because large-scale label certification remains unresolved with the available real-trained gate, we release the soft-mask preset as the default. Text conditioning is supplied by a taxonomy-driven Prompt Atlas that expands one domain specification into a stratified, CLIP-validated prompt bank and transfers to new defect classes without code changes. From the real training images, the pipeline produces 1,020 synthetic candidates, of which 815 pass a CLIP admissibility filter. We evaluate image quality using distributional and fidelity-diversity measures against the real reference set and a Poisson baseline, and audit for out-of-distribution drift and memorization. No single preset dominates; each trades off fidelity, diversity, and label reliability. We therefore release the label-reliable preset as the default and treat a curated mixture as the natural augmentation set. Our claims are limited to image quality, label provenance, and diversity; downstream segmentation is left for future work. Code and an artifact manifest are released for reproducibility.
papers.Reasons for match: Uses diffusion models for synthetic image generation of defects, directly transferable to astronomical anomaly detection and data augmentation.
papers.Short digest: This paper asks how to generate synthetic images of sand boils for low-resource earthen-levee inspection. It uses Stable Diffusion XL fine-tuned with DreamBooth and a multi-branch ControlNet stack, conditioned on text prompts from a taxonomy-driven Prompt Atlas. The main result is a pipeline that produces 1,020 synthetic candidates, with 815 passing a CLIP admissibility filter, enabling label-proven segmentation masks. For astronomy, this method could be directly applied to generate synthetic images of rare astronomical phenomena (e.g., little red dots, high-redshift galaxies, AGN) for training detection models. The pipeline's soft-mask inpainting protocol could preserve real defect pixels while re-rendering backgrounds, analogous to inserting simulated galaxies into real survey images. The caveat is that the method is designed for terrestrial inspection images and may require retraining on astronomical data, and the label certification issue remains unresolved.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the soft-mask inpainting protocol can be adapted to astronomical image formats (e.g., FITS with WCS).
Look for details on the Prompt Atlas construction—could this be replaced with an astronomical taxonomy?
See if the CLIP admissibility filter is calibrated for domain-specific image distributions (e.g., JWST vs. optical).
Evaluate whether the label-proven segmentation masks are truly reliable for training detection models.

papers.title: Integrating Large Language Models and Graph Convolutional Networks for Semi-Supervised Image Classification
papers.authors: Camila Piscioneri Magalhães , Lucas Pascotti Valem
papers.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
papers.abstract: While the growing availability of image data has driven significant advances, labeling datasets remains costly and time-consuming. Therefore, semi-supervised approaches such as Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), which learn from both labeled and unlabeled data, have emerged as a promising solution. One of the primary challenges in applying GCNs to image classification is graph construction, since, unlike in citation networks or similar domains, images typically do not come with a predefined structural representation. For visual data, most studies construct graphs based on the similarity between feature vectors from pretrained deep learning backbones, typically by employing kNN or reciprocal kNN algorithms. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capability in capturing high-level semantics, their integration with GCNs for image classification remains underexplored. Aiming to fill this gap, our approach uses a Vision Language Model (VLM) to generate textual image descriptions, which are then processed by an LLM to estimate semantic similarity scores between connected images. These scores guide the pruning of edges in kNN and reciprocal kNN graphs, filtering out semantically irrelevant neighbors. Experimental results reveal that leveraging LLMs for graph refinement can improve classification accuracy, particularly for kNN graphs and some backbones. The source code is publicly available at this http URL .
papers.Reasons for match: Combines LLMs and graph convolutional networks for semi-supervised image classification, which could be relevant for astronomical source classification with limited labels. The use of VLMs for generating descriptions and LLMs for semantic similarity is interesting.
papers.Short digest: This paper addresses semi-supervised image classification by integrating LLMs and graph convolutional networks. It uses a VLM to generate textual descriptions of images, then an LLM to estimate semantic similarity for graph refinement. This approach could be applied to astronomical image classification where labeled data is scarce. For example, one could use it to classify galaxy morphologies or identify rare objects with limited training examples. A limitation is that the method relies on pretrained VLMs and LLMs that may not be optimized for astronomical images, and the graph construction may need adaptation for large survey datasets.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the VLM used (e.g., CLIP) can generate meaningful descriptions for astronomical images.
Look for experiments on datasets with characteristics similar to astronomical data (e.g., fine-grained classes, imbalanced distributions).
Examine the graph construction and pruning method to see if it scales to large datasets.
